vignette:
Naveen is a 29-year-old shopowner whose family has run a small grocery store in a suburban strip mall for two decades. He took over the shop three years ago, and it's where he spends most of his waking hours. Now, though, he finds himself scanning the aisles even when there are no customers, his shoulders tight, his eyes fixed on the entrance. He tells me he used to enjoy the quiet routine of stocking shelves and chatting with regulars. These days, certain voices or sudden footsteps make his stomach drop before he can stop it.

He came to therapy several weeks ago at the urging of his girlfriend, Priya. He was reluctant. He still struggles to explain what happened, because the story feels improbable to him: a young man, physically strong, letting himself be hurt by the woman he loved. The abuse began about a year into their relationship, during a minor disagreement. She slapped him. He was stunned-too shocked to react-and then apologized for upsetting her. Over the next several months, the slaps turned into closed fists, and the apologies from her became accusations that he had provoked her. He started walking on eggshells, second-guessing every word. He never fought back. "I thought if I just took it, she'd see I was trying to make it work," he says.

The worst incident happened eight months ago, on a Friday night. They were at her apartment. She accused him of flirting with a female customer at his shop. He denied it, and she began hitting him across the face and chest. He tried to leave, but she blocked the door. He ended up on the floor, curled into a ball, as she kicked his ribs. He still has a faint scar on his forearm from where a glass vase shattered and cut him. After that night, he broke up with her, blocked her number, and hasn't seen her since. But the silence inside his shop has become a different kind of noise.

Naveen now struggles with a constant sense of dread. When a customer's voice rises even slightly-asking for a refund, complaining about a price-his heart pounds so hard he can't hear their words for a few seconds. He has stopped going to the bank on the same street where she used to park her car. He goes to a different ATM three blocks away, even though it takes longer. At night, he dreams of being pinned against a wall, unable to move, and wakes up with his fists clenched. He has begun drinking two or three beers after closing to numb the restlessness, but the images of her face stay.

His relationship with Priya is suffering. He loves her, but when she reaches for him in bed, he freezes. He worries she will see the scar on his forearm and ask questions he can't answer. He has started snapping at her for small things-leaving a light on, speaking too loudly on the phone-and then feels a shame so heavy it keeps him from apologizing. In session, he often looks at the floor, rubbing his hands together. "I'm supposed to be the one who's in control," he says. "I own a business. I'm the one people count on. How do I tell anyone I let a woman beat me up?" He laughs dryly, but his eyes are wet.

He has not told his parents, aunts, or cousins. In his community, a man who is abused is seen as weak, and a man who complains about his partner is seen as ungrateful. So Naveen keeps the story locked inside the shop, where he can arrange the cans of chickpeas and bags of rice into neat, predictable rows. It is the only thing he can still control.
